To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ERalpha and ERalpha are expressed in breast cancer and surrounding normal tissues and ERalpha is dysregulated in breast tumours.

the mRNA expression levels of ERalpha and ERalpha protein expression in breast cancer are higher than those of ERbeta, while the mRNA expression levels and the protein expression of ERbeta are more similar in breast cancer and in normal tissues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular characterisation of ERalpha and ERalpha in human breast cancer, and provides a basis for further studies on the role of ERalpha and/or ERbeta in breast carcinogenesis.
the expression of ERalpha and ER beta at the mRNA and at protein level and with their localisation in human breast cancer and normal tissues.
the expression of oestrogen receptor isoforms in human breast cancer, and their relationship to clinicopathological factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ERalpha is the main oestrogen-regulated gene in breast cancer, while ERbeta is more likely a modulating factor in breast carcinogenesis.

both ERalpha and ER beta are expressed in human primary breast cancers and their expression levels are correlated with the expression of proliferation marker Ki- 67, but not with the expression of ERalpha and ER-beta mRNA levels.
ERbeta is more stable in breast cancer than ERalpha, and the expression of ERalpha is more sensitive to the tumour microenvironment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression of ERalpha is more heterogeneous in breast cancer than ERbeta.
ERalpha is a more sensitive marker for breast cancer than ERbeta and ERbeta is more sensitive for normal breast tissue than ERalpha.

there are distinct mRNA and protein expression patterns of ERalpha and ER beta in breast cancers, and the expression of ERalpha is associated with age, proliferation marker Ki- 67, and progesterone receptor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is an association between ERalpha expression and clinicopathological features of primary breast cancer, which may have a role in breast cancer development.
the expression of ERalpha and ER beta are regulated differently in breast tumour and normal breast tissue.
the amount of ERalpha mRNA and the amount of ERbeta mRNA are not necessarily correlated with the amount of ER protein.
